clinician.final_diagnosis: Transient acetylcholine receptor-related myasthenia gravis occurring shortly after MIS-C
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 7-year-old previously well girl presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, cough, diarrhea, and headaches, progressing to shock (BP 65/53 mm Hg, HR 135 beats/min, cold extremities, capillary refill >3 seconds, temperature 39.5°C). Clinical examination revealed bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis, erythematous desquamating rash on abdomen/back/neck, and hand/foot swelling—findings consistent with MIS-C. Laboratory studies on admission demonstrated leucocytosis with neutrophilia and lymphopenia (WBC 24.0×10⁹/L, neutrophil 94.2%, lymphocyte 2.4%), anemia (Hb 10.5 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (platelets 122×10⁹/L), markedly elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 292 mg/L, ferritin 1022 μg/L, D-dimer 11.65 mg/L, LDH 517 u/L), acute kidney injury (urea 22.1 mmol/L, creatinine 259 μmol/L, hyponatremia 126 mmol/L, hypokalemia 3.2 mmol/L), and markedly elevated cardiac enzymes (troponin T 477 ng/L, pro-BNP 98,900 ng/L). SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative but IgG antibodies to N protein were positive, indicating recent infection. Echocardiography showed reduced left ventricular function with mildly dilated left ventricle and markedly reduced ejection fraction of 38%, with no coronary aneurysms. She was admitted to PICU. Following PICU discharge, she developed myalgia and marked proximal muscle weakness (lower limbs more affected: proximal 2/5, distal 3/5; upper limbs: proximal 3/5, distal 4/5), with positive Gower sign, waddling gait, and compensatory lumbar lordosis. Seventy-two hours post-PICU discharge, she developed fluctuating and fatigable bilateral ptosis with impairment of upward gaze, mild diplopia, positive curtain sign, and positive Cogan eyelid twitch test—classic features of myasthenia gravis. Acetylcholine receptor antibody testing was positive (0.51 nm/L), confirming the diagnosis. She was treated with pyridostigmine and corticosteroids. One month post-discharge, the ptosis had completely resolved with marked improvement in proximal muscle weakness. Repeat acetylcholine receptor antibody testing was negative, and both pyridostigmine and corticosteroids were slowly discontinued, confirming the transient nature of the myasthenia gravis.
